summary.text:
The best rate cross-check we have had. Shropshire's Appendix A gives five PWLB certainty rates at the close of 31 March 2026 — 1yr 5.04%, 5yr 5.28%, 10yr 5.72%, 25yr 6.29%, 50yr 6.08% — and our own series gives the same five figures for the same day, to the basis point. Northumberland and Tameside independently corroborate two of them.

The position: borrowing rose from £420.205m to £459.705m against a CFR of £517m, leaving about £57m internal and closing fast. £100m was drawn across nine PWLB loans between 24 February and 31 March 2026 at 4.32% to 5.09%, every one of them with a maturity of 18 to 66 months. Appendix A says why: short 'so that the Council can take advantage of reductions in interest rates in the next 2-5 years'. 30% of the whole book now reprices within two years. £61.8m of that borrowing is Exceptional Financial Support, costing £4.964m a year, and a £45.6m DSG deficit is being carried on cash balances until the High Needs Stability Grant lands.

Worth saying plainly: Shropshire had already caught the turn. Appendix A records that at the start of April 2026 the market expected Bank Rate to rise to 4% or 4.25%. This is not a council that needs telling which way rates went — it is one that has a lot riding on when they come back.

officer.subject: 30% of your debt reprices inside two years
officer.body:
Hi Cheryl,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit and Governance on 25 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

I should start with a compliment that's also our cross-check. Appendix A gives five PWLB certainty rates at the close of 31 March — 1yr 5.04%, 5yr 5.28%, 10yr 5.72%, 25yr 6.29%, 50yr 6.08% — and our own series gives all five for the same day, to the basis point. We read a lot of these and it's rare to find five in a row that tie. Appendix A also records that by early April the market expected Bank Rate at 4% or 4.25% rather than falling, which is the right read and one plenty of reports written later still hadn't caught up with.

So this isn't a note about which way rates went. It's about the shape of what you've built. £100m drawn across nine loans between 24 February and 31 March, every one of them at 18 to 66 months, and Appendix A says plainly why — short, to take advantage of reductions in two to five years. Thirty per cent of the whole book now reprices inside two years, and on our side £117.9m of your PWLB loans mature in that window. £61.8m of it is Exceptional Financial Support at £4.964m a year, running alongside a £45.6m DSG deficit carried on cash until the High Needs Stability Grant lands.

Where that lands depends entirely on the curve at each rollover. Today's certainty rates are 5.06% at two years and 5.34% at five, against the 4.32% to 5.09% you drew at. The long end has moved a touch further: fifty-year is 6.27% now against your 6.08% at 31 March. We're not going to pretend to know where it goes next, but it's the sort of thing worth watching weekly rather than at the next report, which is what the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard is for — both fixings, whole curve, ten seconds. We also hold 51 of your PWLB loans at 31 March, £451.85m of the £459.705m total, priced daily against the DMO repayment curve so premiums and discounts are a lookup: pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. And the monthly sector breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is a useful read on how thin the market is before you roll.

On training, three fit Shropshire: Interest rate risk and Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the short-dated third of the book; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
